claims.claim: Bryce Lynch's own list of what he looks for in an adventure module states that boxed text is usually not a good thing.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, 'Review Standards', tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: Boxed text is usually not a good thing.

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch lists a terse writing style among the qualities he looks for in an adventure module.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, 'Review Standards', tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: Terse writing style

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch lists evocative atmosphere among the qualities he looks for in an adventure module.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, 'Review Standards', tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: Evocative atmosphere.

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch's standards reject epic backstory in an adventure module and ask only for enough to start play.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, 'Review Standards', tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: I don’t care about your epic backstory.

claims.claim: The phrase 'succinct and evocative' on tenfootpole.org is the top grade for Language on a second reviewer's rating scale (signed 'The Pretty Girl'), not a line of Bryce Lynch's own standards.
claims.source: 'The Pretty Girl' (second reviewer), rating scale on tenfootpole.org 'Review Standards'
claims.quote: Succinct and evocative
claims.page: Review Standards, 'The Pretty Girl' scale, Language 4

claims.claim: On that same Language scale the lowest grade is reserved for writing that is very wordy or incomprehensible.
claims.source: 'The Pretty Girl' (second reviewer), rating scale on tenfootpole.org 'Review Standards'
claims.quote: Very wordy/ incomprehensible
claims.page: Review Standards, 'The Pretty Girl' scale, Language 0

claims.claim: In a comment on his own standards page Bryce Lynch says he loathes overly long backstory and fiction introductions.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, comment of 19 April 2016 on tenfootpole.org 'Review Standards'
claims.quote: I LOATHE the overly long backstory

claims.claim: Justin Alexander judges the location keys of published adventures to be almost universally terrible.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: almost universally terrible

claims.claim: Justin Alexander defines boxed text as prewritten text designed to be read aloud by the GM.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: prewritten text designed to be read aloud by the GM
claims.page: Art of the Key, 'The Era of Boxed Text'

claims.claim: Justin Alexander dates the first appearance of read-aloud boxed text to Lost Tamoachan and hedges between 1979 and 1980.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: In either 1979 or 1980
claims.page: Art of the Key, 'The Era of Boxed Text'

claims.claim: Justin Alexander argues a room key must sequence information by what the players meet first, so a room with an ogre in the middle of it leads with the ogre.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: should talk about the ogre first
claims.page: Art of the Key, 'Adventure Formatting Guides'

claims.claim: Justin Alexander argues that a rigid adventure format defeats its own aim of making information easy to parse and reference.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: a rigid format ends up having the opposite effect
claims.page: Art of the Key, closing of Part 1

claims.claim: Justin Alexander says the standardized 3rd Edition adventure format encourages writers to fill the format with text that is not needed.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: it tends to encourage writers to “fill the format”
claims.page: Art of the Key, 'Adventure Formatting Guides'

claims.claim: Justin Alexander labels the dense undifferentiated paragraph key that TSR used for most of a decade the Gygax wall of text.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: the Gygax “wall of text” key
claims.page: Art of the Key, 'A Brief History of the Key'

claims.claim: Justin Alexander's prescribed key opens with the information a character perceives on entering, which he calls seen in a glance.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key - Part 2', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: seen in a glance

claims.claim: Justin Alexander's alternative to a fixed key format is to order the entry by the sequence in which information will be wanted at the table.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key - Part 2', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: focus on the sequencing of information

claims.claim: Justin Alexander tells key writers to move from the general to the specific as the players investigate.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key - Part 2', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: move from the general to the specific

claims.claim: Justin Alexander bolds the name of each significant element in a room so the GM can find the matching information quickly.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key - Part 2', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: the bold title makes it easy to find the information

claims.feature: other: background and history in a key
claims.claim: Justin Alexander confines a location's history and former use to a GM Background tag that must be brief and infrequently needed.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key - Part 2', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: It should be brief, to the point, and infrequently needed.

claims.claim: Justin Alexander credits the delve format with the single good idea that everything the GM needs is on the page.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key - Part 3', The Alexandrian, 2016
claims.quote: Everything you need is on the page.

claims.claim: Justin Alexander grants that boxed text virtually guarantees essential information is not accidentally omitted in play.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls', The Alexandrian, 2022
claims.quote: will virtually guarantee that it’s not accidentally omitted

claims.claim: Justin Alexander counts inflexibility as an inherent cost of prewritten boxed text, since one passage must serve every approach and condition.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls', The Alexandrian, 2022
claims.quote: The result is inherently less flexible.
claims.page: GM Don't List #13, 'So why wouldn't you use boxed text?'

claims.claim: Justin Alexander names freeze-frame boxed text as the failure in which the world keeps moving while the characters stand frozen.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls', The Alexandrian, 2022
claims.quote: PCs are frozen in place while a bunch of stuff happens
claims.page: GM Don't List #13, 'Sins of the Box'

claims.claim: Justin Alexander names the reaction point as the place in a description past which the world must not move without the players.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls', The Alexandrian, 2022
claims.quote: What we’ve identified here is the reaction point
claims.page: GM Don't List #13, 'Sins of the Box'

claims.claim: Justin Alexander condemns remote-control boxed text, which declares the thoughts, feelings or actions of the player characters.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls', The Alexandrian, 2022
claims.quote: declaring the thoughts or feelings or (worse yet!) actions of the PCs

claims.claim: Justin Alexander's rule for read-aloud text is to show the scene and never to tell the players how they are reacting to it.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls', The Alexandrian, 2022
claims.quote: Don’t tell them how they’re reacting to it.

claims.claim: A reader commenting on the Alexandrian recalls a lost Wizards devblog article whose thesis was that GM description should never run past three sentences.
claims.source: Reader comment by 'mellonbread', 2 August 2022, on The Alexandrian
claims.quote: should never be longer than three sentences
claims.confidence: medium: a reader's recollection of an article he says was deleted; the surviving 2005 Wizards article gives two sentences, not three

claims.claim: David Hartlage dates the introduction of boxed text descriptions read by the DM on entry to Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan in 1979.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'Picturing the dungeon - boxed text', DMDavid, 2012
claims.quote: In 1979, Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan introduced boxed text descriptions

claims.claim: David Hartlage attributes the original purpose of boxed text to giving every table the same play experience in tournament competition.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'Picturing the dungeon - boxed text', DMDavid, 2012
claims.quote: a consistent play experience in a competitive environment

claims.claim: David Hartlage reports that in a tournament the significant detail was placed among less important ones in the boxed text and his team missed it.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'Picturing the dungeon - boxed text', DMDavid, 2012
claims.quote: the text mentioned the runes alongside other, less important details

claims.claim: David Hartlage says a reader's voice takes a different tone and cadence from extemporaneous speech, and that monotony lets players' attention wander.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'Picturing the dungeon - boxed text', DMDavid, 2012
claims.quote: their voice takes a different tone and cadence

claims.claim: David Hartlage defends boxed text as still the best available summary of what players must learn on entering a room.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'Picturing the dungeon - boxed text', DMDavid, 2012
claims.quote: No one has shown a better way to summarize

claims.claim: David Hartlage says that when he knows the material well he paraphrases the boxed text rather than reading it.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'Picturing the dungeon - boxed text', DMDavid, 2012
claims.quote: I paraphrase boxed text

claims.claim: David Noonan reports that from watching Gen Con 2005 tables a DM reading aloud holds attention for two sentences.
claims.source: David Noonan (with Jesse Decker), 'Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast Design & Development, 2005
claims.quote: If you’re the DM, you get two sentences. Period.

claims.claim: The same Wizards article labels its own Gen Con observation qualitative rather than a controlled measurement.
claims.source: David Noonan (with Jesse Decker), 'Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast Design & Development, 2005
claims.quote: this kind of “research” is pretty qualitative
claims.page: Here's the Plan: We're Going Undercover!

claims.claim: David Noonan's explanation for the attention loss is that boxed text substitutes oration for the conversation that a game normally is.
claims.source: David Noonan (with Jesse Decker), 'Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast Design & Development, 2005
claims.quote: Boxed text replaces that conversation with oration.

claims.claim: David Noonan describes a D&D game as at heart a conversation between the DM and the players.
claims.source: David Noonan (with Jesse Decker), 'Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast Design & Development, 2005
claims.quote: At its heart, a D&D game is a conversation.

claims.claim: David Noonan's prior hypothesis, which the watching exceeded, was that boxed text longer than a paragraph is not worth reading.
claims.source: David Noonan (with Jesse Decker), 'Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast Design & Development, 2005
claims.quote: boxed text longer than a paragraph probably isn’t worth reading

claims.claim: Writing for Wizards of the Coast in 2005, David Noonan advises DMs to ditch the boxed text and describe the room in their own words.
claims.source: David Noonan (with Jesse Decker), 'Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast Design & Development, 2005
claims.quote: ditch the boxed text and use your own words
claims.page: Beyond the door, you see a format change

claims.claim: David Noonan observes that boxed text in Wizards adventures had become markedly shorter by 2005 than in earlier products.
claims.source: David Noonan (with Jesse Decker), 'Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast Design & Development, 2005
claims.quote: Boxed text in adventures used to be a lot longer

claims.claim: James Maliszewski reports that Gygax attributed his own voice to the old fashioned books he read as a boy rather than to Jack Vance.
claims.source: James Maliszewski relaying a private conversation with Gary Gygax, 'High Gygaxian', Grognardia, 2009
claims.quote: old fashioned
claims.confidence: medium: a blogger's paraphrase of a private conversation; only the two quoted words are Gygax's

claims.claim: In the same account Gygax credited a lifelong love of dictionaries and thesauruses for his vocabulary.
claims.source: James Maliszewski relaying a private conversation with Gary Gygax, 'High Gygaxian', Grognardia, 2009
claims.quote: his lifelong love of dictionaries and thesauruses

claims.claim: James Maliszewski reports that Gygax demurred when told his voice was a dialect of Jack Vance's.
claims.source: James Maliszewski, 'High Gygaxian', Grognardia, 2009
claims.quote: I once told Gary my opinion on this and he demurred

claims.claim: James Maliszewski contrasts Gygax's florid prose with modern game books, which he says read like technical manuals.
claims.source: James Maliszewski, 'High Gygaxian', Grognardia, 2009
claims.quote: Modern game books read like what they are: technical manuals.

claims.claim: James Maliszewski holds up Gygax's description of the Vault of the Drow as more evocative than the place descriptions in contemporary adventures.
claims.source: James Maliszewski, 'High Gygaxian', Grognardia, 2009
claims.quote: you'll find few passages in contemporary adventures that are as evocative

claims.claim: Dyson Logos tells OSR adventure writers to get rid of boxed text.
claims.source: Dyson Logos, 'The Dreaded Boxed Text', Dyson's Dodecahedron, 2013
claims.quote: So, OSR adventure writers, get rid of the boxed text.

claims.claim: Dyson Logos proposes replacing read-aloud prose with a point-form list of the things seen in the room, so the DM can present them conversationally.
claims.source: Dyson Logos, 'The Dreaded Boxed Text', Dyson's Dodecahedron, 2013
claims.quote: replace it with a point-form list of things seen in the room

claims.claim: Dyson Logos traces the arrival of read-aloud text in the 1e era to the tournament use of the early published adventures.
claims.source: Dyson Logos, 'The Dreaded Boxed Text', Dyson's Dodecahedron, 2013
claims.quote: I tend to blame this on the tournament usage
claims.confidence: medium: the author frames it as his own supposition
